reasoning: The person is asking for something to be done now — make a pass over the prover's skill — so this is an instruction, and it is accepted as work. The word 'only' is not a second act: nothing is in flight for it to halt or correct, and it says nothing the instruction's own goal does not already carry — it is the scope of the one thing asked for, not a separate clause. So one act, one new piece of work: a pass over one skill is a single result someone could want on its own, however many places inside that skill it touches. It touches documentation and communication, because the skill body is the text that changes; and product value and behaviour, because that body is what the prover actually does when it runs, so revising it revises the behaviour. Nothing changes in architecture, in the user's path, in analytics, or in release, so those are not named. Specialists: a developer, because the pass ends in edits to the skill, and an independent verifier, because a review's own findings should be checked against the skill by someone who did not write them. No spec author unless the pass turns up behaviour the spec does not already describe, and no test author — there is no regression to choose evidence for yet.
